trivial

/TRIV-ee-ul/ — rhymes with "drivel" · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Trivial describes something of little importance or significance.

They argued for an hour over a trivial detail: the color of the napkins.

Example

They argued for an hour over a trivial detail: the color of the napkins.

Trivial means something of little importance or significance. In this sentence, the color of napkins is trivial—it's a minor detail that shouldn't really matter. Yet they spent a full hour arguing about it! Using trivial emphasizes how unimportant this detail is compared to the time wasted. A plainer word like "small" wouldn't carry that judgment; trivial makes clear this detail should be ignored.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

minor: Minor means smaller and less serious than other things of its kind — a minor injury, a minor delay. A minor issue still counts and may need attention later. Trivial goes further: it judges a thing too unimportant to deserve attention at all. Minor ranks it low; trivial dismisses it.

insignificant: Insignificant means too small to make any real difference — an insignificant error changes nothing about the result. Trivial is a judgment about worth rather than effect: a trivial detail may change something slightly, yet it still does not deserve anyone's time. Insignificant measures impact; trivial measures whether it merits attention.

petty: Petty points at people, not things: a petty person fusses over unimportant matters and keeps score of tiny slights. Trivial describes the matter itself — of little importance or significance. A dispute over napkin colors is trivial; the cousin who sulks about it for a week is being petty.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

crucial: important enough to decide the outcome

momentous: of great and lasting importance

Where it sits · how much it matters — inconsequential → meaningful → vital → trivial

inconsequential vs. trivial: Inconsequential is even weaker than trivial: a trivial detail matters very little, while an inconsequential one has no effect at all.

meaningful vs. trivial: Meaningful sits above trivial on the importance scale: a trivial matter can be safely ignored, but a meaningful one deserves real attention.

vital vs. trivial: Vital lies at the far opposite end from trivial — a trivial detail barely matters, while a vital one is essential to success.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — tri-

Prefix — tri-: three (Latin)

Root — vi

Root — vi: road, way (Latin via) (Latin)

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to (adjective-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Tri- ('three') + vi ('road') + -al: trivial originally described the everyday chatter heard at a spot where three roads met — the kind of commonplace street-corner talk that came to mean unimportant.

Use the root in a new word: deviate

Use the root in a new word: deviate: When hikers deviate from the trail, they leave the road they were following — the same Latin root via ('road') hidden inside trivial, which began as talk at a three-road crossing.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / informal

Use trivial to describe something that is unimportant or insignificant—often with the hint that people shouldn't waste time on it. It's a judgment word, not just a size descriptor: "small" describes only size; "trivial" says something isn't worth your attention. In formal writing, trivial is clear and respected. In casual speech, you might just say "doesn't matter."
